title: JESUS SAID, “LOVE YOUR ENEMIES”… SO WHY ARE SOME CHRISTIANS CHEERING WHEN THEIR ENEMIES SUFFER?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “LOVE YOUR ENEMIES”… SO WHY ARE SOME CHRISTIANS CHEERING WHEN THEIR ENEMIES SUFFER?

When someone who wounded you finally falls, is that God's justice you're celebrating—or is it the revenge you've been secretly praying for? The answer may reveal something about your heart that you never wanted to confront.
There is a kind of happiness that should frighten us.
Not because happiness is wrong.
But because sometimes the thing making us happy is another human being's suffering.
Someone who betrayed you loses everything.
Someone who humiliated you gets publicly exposed.
Someone who destroyed your reputation watches their own reputation collapse.
Someone who made your life miserable suddenly finds themselves drowning in the very pain they once caused you.
And somewhere deep inside, a quiet voice whispers…
Good. Now they know how it feels.
You don't say it out loud. Maybe you don't even want to admit you're thinking it.
But something inside you feels satisfied.
Then you open Facebook.

You see Christians sharing the news. Some are laughing. Others are posting sarcastic comments. A few are quoting Scripture about judgment. Someone writes, "God doesn't sleep!" Another declares, "Touch not God's anointed!" Others flood the comments with laughing emojis and declarations that their enemy finally got what they deserved.
And perhaps the most disturbing part isn't that unbelievers are watching Christians celebrate someone's downfall.
It's that we have become so comfortable doing it that we no longer recognize the contradiction.
We worship a Savior who prayed for His executioners.
Yet sometimes we cannot resist celebrating when someone who offended us gets what we believe is coming to them.
And before you decide this article is about somebody else…
Remember the last person whose suffering secretly made you smile.
Because this isn't simply about the cruelty of people on social media.
It's about the dangerous possibility that we can carry a Bible in our hands while carrying revenge in our hearts.
And Jesus has something to say about that.
Something that may hurt before it heals.
In Matthew 5:44, Jesus says:
"But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you." (Matthew 5:44, KJV)
Those words sound beautiful when printed on a church wall.
They become much harder when the enemy has a face.
A face you remember.
A voice that still echoes in your mind.
A name that can ruin your peace just by appearing on your phone.
Jesus wasn't speaking about loving people who merely disagree with our opinions. He was calling His disciples to love people who actively opposed, mistreated, and persecuted them.
The Greek text of Matthew 5:44 contains the command:
ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
Agapate tous echthrous hymōn.
"Love your enemies."
The verb agapate comes from agapaō, meaning to love. In this context, it is a command, not a suggestion. And the word echthrous refers to enemies—people who are hostile toward you.
Jesus did not command His followers to pretend evil was good.
He did not command them to trust dangerous people.
He did not command abused people to return to abusive relationships.
He commanded something far more demanding.
He commanded us to refuse to let hatred determine how we treat another human being.

And the command continues in the earliest Greek textual tradition of this verse with the instruction to pray for those who persecute us. The longer wording familiar from the King James Version also appears in Luke 6:27–28, where Jesus explicitly teaches doing good to those who hate us and blessing those who curse us.
The point is unmistakable.
Jesus does not merely ask us to stop attacking our enemies.
He calls us to seek their good.
Even when they have done us wrong.
Even when justice is necessary.
Even when reconciliation is not yet possible.
And that is where our hearts begin to resist.
Because if we're being painfully honest, sometimes we don't want our enemies restored.
We want them exposed.
We want them embarrassed.
We want them to experience the loneliness we experienced.
We want someone to finally recognize how much damage they caused.
And underneath all those desires may be one wounded cry:
I just want somebody to understand what they did to me.
That longing is not difficult to understand.
Perhaps someone betrayed your marriage.
Perhaps a family member treated you like you were worthless.
Perhaps a church leader abused your trust, and when you spoke up, people defended the leader instead of listening to your pain.
Perhaps you were falsely accused, abandoned by people you loved, or publicly humiliated by someone who never apologized.
You prayed.
You cried.
You tried to forgive.
But the wounds remained.
Then one day you heard that the person who hurt you was suffering.
And for the first time in a long time, it felt as though the scales had finally tipped in your favor.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
God does not require you to call injustice acceptable. But He does call you to surrender your desire to become the author of someone else's destruction.
Those are two very different things.
The Bible does not teach that love means the absence of justice.
It teaches that love and justice must never be separated from God's righteousness.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." (KJV)
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that wrongdoing doesn't matter.
He does not say perpetrators should escape accountability.
He does not say victims must remain silent.
He tells believers not to take personal vengeance, because judgment ultimately belongs to God.
And immediately afterward, Paul writes:
Think about how shocking that is.
The person who harmed you is hungry.
And instead of enjoying their hunger, you are commanded to feed them.
The person who made you suffer is thirsty.
And instead of celebrating their desperation, you are told to give them water.
This is not the natural response of a wounded human heart.
This is what the grace of Jesus begins producing in a surrendered heart.
And perhaps this is why some Christians struggle so deeply with the command.
We love the idea of receiving grace.
But sometimes we resent the possibility of our enemies receiving it.
We want mercy when our own sins are exposed.
We want justice when someone else's sins are exposed.
We want God to remember our repentance.
But we want Him to remember every detail of what they did.
And somewhere along the way, we begin acting as though the blood of Jesus is precious when it covers us, but offensive when it is offered to the people who wounded us.
That is a frightening place for a Christian heart to live.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people are finally rewarded while bad people are destroyed.
It is the announcement that sinners who deserve judgment can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
And that includes sinners like us.
Before we were victims of another person's wrongdoing, we were already people in need of God's mercy.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
And Romans 5:10 goes even further.
It says that we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies.
Enemies.
Let that word settle.
The very category of people Jesus commands us to love is the category Scripture uses to describe our former relationship with God.
And what did Jesus do for His enemies?
He went to the cross.
He did not wait for us to become worthy before demonstrating His love.
He did not demand that we repair ourselves before making salvation possible.
He died for sinners, and through His resurrection He opened the way for repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life.
This does not mean everyone is automatically saved regardless of their response to Christ. Scripture calls people to repent and believe the Gospel.
But it does mean that God's mercy reaches toward people who could never earn it.
And if we have received that mercy, how can we treat the possibility of someone else's repentance as an insult?
There is an Old Testament verse that should make every Christian reconsider the way we respond when an enemy falls.
Proverbs 24:17 says:
"Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth." (KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
בִּנְפֹל אוֹיִבְךָ אַל־תִּשְׂמָח
Binfol oyivkha al-tismach.
"When your enemy falls, do not rejoice."
The Hebrew verb tismach comes from samach, meaning to rejoice or be glad. With the negative command al, the instruction is clear: do not take delight in your enemy's downfall.
Not merely, "Don't post about it."
Not merely, "Don't laugh where people can see you."
The following line reaches into the heart itself.
Do not let your heart be glad when your enemy stumbles.
God is addressing something deeper than public behavior.
He is addressing secret satisfaction.
The private celebration.
The hidden pleasure.
The moment when another person's pain feels like emotional compensation for your own.
And here is the question that exposes us:
If your enemy genuinely repented, turned to Jesus, and experienced restoration, would you rejoice—or would you feel cheated?
Don't rush past that.
Imagine the person who wounded you standing before God, broken over their sin.
Imagine them confessing what they did without excuses.
Imagine them accepting responsibility, making appropriate restitution where possible, and seeking forgiveness.
Imagine their life being transformed by Christ.
Would you praise God?
Or would something inside you whisper…
After everything they did, they don't deserve another chance.
If the second response feels familiar, you may understand Jonah more than you realize.
Jonah was sent to Nineveh, a city associated with the Assyrian empire, whose brutality made it a deeply troubling enemy in Israel's history.
God commanded Jonah to proclaim judgment against the city.
But when the Ninevites responded with repentance, God relented from the announced destruction.
And Jonah was furious.
Not because God's mercy had failed.
But because God's mercy had succeeded.
Jonah 4:1 says:
"But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." (KJV)
Imagine that.
A prophet of God was angry because people repented and were spared.
He knew God was gracious and merciful.
He simply didn't want that mercy extended to those people.
How many of us have carried Jonah's heart into our own conflicts?
We want revival.
But not for that person.
We want forgiveness preached.
But we secretly hope our enemies will face humiliation first.
We want the lost to come home.
But when the lost person has hurt us, we become uncomfortable with how wide the Father's mercy can reach.
And God asks Jonah a question that still confronts us:
"Doest thou well to be angry?" (Jonah 4:4, KJV)
In other words, is your anger justified in the way you are holding it?
It is possible to be right about someone else's wrongdoing and still be wrong about what their suffering produces in your heart.
It is possible to recognize injustice and become consumed by vengeance.
It is possible to defend truth while slowly losing compassion.
And it is possible to speak constantly about God's judgment while forgetting that His kindness leads sinners toward repentance, as Romans 2:4 teaches.
But we need to be careful here.
There is a difference between rejoicing that evil has been stopped and rejoicing that a human being is suffering.
When an abuser is removed from a position of power, protecting the vulnerable is good.
When a corrupt official is held accountable, justice matters.
When a predator is convicted through a fair legal process, the protection of victims is not cruelty.
When lies are exposed, truth deserves to be honored.
Scripture does not command us to mourn the continued success of wickedness.
Psalm 97:10 tells those who love the Lord to hate evil.
Amos 5:24 calls for justice to flow like a mighty stream.
Romans 13 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in punishing wrongdoing.
And Revelation portrays God's final judgment as righteous.
Therefore, we must not twist "love your enemies" into a command to protect abusers, silence victims, obstruct accountability, or deny the seriousness of sin.
Forgiveness is not permission for someone to keep hurting you.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Reconciliation requires truth, and where serious harm has occurred, genuine repentance, accountability, and safety matter.
You may forgive someone and still maintain distance.
You may pray for someone's salvation and still report their crime.
You may desire their repentance and still testify truthfully about what happened.
You may refuse hatred while refusing to give them access to your life.
Love is not the abandonment of wisdom.
Grace is not the cancellation of consequences.
And mercy is not the enemy of justice.
But here is where we must examine ourselves.
When a person faces legitimate consequences, are we grateful that harm has been stopped?
Or are we feeding ourselves on their humiliation?
When someone is exposed, do we care about truth, victims, accountability, and repentance?
Or do we keep replaying the scandal because watching them fall gives us pleasure?
When we share a story online, are we helping people understand what happened?
Or are we inviting a crowd to mock someone we already despise?
The difference may not always be obvious to the people watching.
But God sees the heart.
And social media has made it dangerously easy to turn another person's suffering into entertainment.
A screenshot becomes a weapon.
A tragedy becomes a joke.
A scandal becomes a competition for the cruelest comment.
A Christian who has never spoken a word to the suffering person suddenly becomes an expert on what God is doing in their life.
"They're being punished by God!"
"That's what happens when you fight God's people!"
"God finally got them!"
But how do we know?
How can we confidently declare that every illness, financial collapse, accident, public embarrassment, or personal tragedy is God's direct punishment for a specific offense?
We cannot.
And Jesus explicitly challenged that kind of reasoning.
In Luke 13:1–5, people brought Him reports of terrible deaths.
Jesus refused the assumption that those who suffered were worse sinners than everyone else.
Instead, He turned the conversation toward the need for repentance among the living.
And in John 9:1–3, when His disciples assumed a man's blindness must have resulted from someone's sin, Jesus rejected their explanation.
These passages do not deny that God judges sin.
They warn us against claiming to know God's hidden purposes behind another person's suffering.
Sometimes suffering results from human wrongdoing.
Sometimes it comes from living in a broken world.
Sometimes consequences follow sinful choices.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a particular tragedy occurred.
We must not pretend to possess divine knowledge that God has not given us.
Because when Christians confidently assign God's punishment to every misfortune that befalls someone they dislike, they risk misrepresenting the very God they claim to defend.
And the people watching may begin to wonder:
If this is how Christians treat their enemies, what happens when I become one of them?
That question should grieve us.
Because the Church is called to proclaim the Gospel of reconciliation, not become a crowd addicted to public humiliation.
Consider the cross.
Not the polished cross hanging in a sanctuary.
The real cross.
The blood.
The nails.
The mockery.
The soldiers gambling for Jesus' clothing.
The religious leaders ridiculing Him.
The crowd watching an innocent man suffer.
And there, in the middle of unimaginable injustice, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." (Luke 23:34, KJV)

This prayer is recorded in many ancient manuscripts, although some early manuscripts omit it, a textual detail noted in modern critical editions. Its message is consistent with Jesus' teaching on loving enemies and with Stephen's prayer for his killers in Acts 7:60.
Jesus was not declaring cruelty harmless.
He was not pretending His executioners had done nothing wrong.
He was praying for mercy in the very place where human hatred was doing its worst.
And when Stephen was being stoned to death, he followed his Savior's example.
He cried:
"Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." (Acts 7:60, KJV)
Think about that.
Stephen did not have a comfortable distance from his enemies.
They were killing him.
And still he prayed.
What kind of power makes that possible?
Not personality.
Not emotional numbness.
Not pretending the pain doesn't exist.
It is the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
The same grace that can take a heart consumed by bitterness and teach it to pray again.
The same grace that can help someone seek justice without becoming cruel.
The same grace that can turn hatred into compassion without denying the seriousness of evil.
And perhaps one of the most astonishing examples of that grace is the apostle Paul.
Before he became a preacher of Christ, Saul persecuted Christians.
Acts 8:3 describes him making havoc of the church, entering houses and committing believers to prison.
Acts 9 portrays him breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord.
Imagine being one of the believers who had lost family, freedom, or security because of Saul's persecution.
Imagine hearing that this man—the man you feared—had encountered Jesus.
And now he claimed to be your brother.
Would you believe him?
Would you trust him?
Would you welcome him immediately?
The early disciples were understandably afraid.
Acts 9:26 says they did not believe he was a disciple.
And that matters.
Their caution was not automatically a failure of love.
Saul's history was real.
Their fear had reasons.
But Barnabas eventually helped bring him before the apostles, explaining what had happened.
And the man who once persecuted the Church became one of its most influential missionaries.
Imagine what would have been lost if the only outcome believers could imagine for Saul was destruction.
Imagine if everyone had insisted that his past made transformation impossible.
The Gospel does not erase the reality of Saul's crimes.
It magnifies the mercy of the Savior who confronted him, humbled him, and changed his life.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy became a brother.
The man who tried to silence the name of Jesus spent the rest of his life proclaiming it.
That is not a sentimental story about overlooking evil.
That is the scandal of grace.
And perhaps that is why the Gospel is so uncomfortable.
Because grace refuses to remain inside the boundaries of the people we consider deserving.
We would gladly celebrate a miracle if God healed someone we loved.
But what if He healed someone we despised?
We would praise God if our child came home after years of rebellion.
But what if the person returning was the one who destroyed our peace?
We would rejoice if a prisoner found Christ.
But what if that prisoner had committed a crime against someone close to us?
Could we desire their genuine salvation while still seeking rightful justice?
That is where Christian love becomes more than a slogan.
And that is where we discover how deeply we still need the Lord to change us.
Maybe you're reading this with a name in your mind.
Someone you haven't forgiven.
Someone whose apology never came.
Someone who continues to live comfortably while you're still rebuilding the pieces of what they broke.
And perhaps you're thinking:
You don't understand what they did to me.
You're right.
I may not know the details.
I won't pretend that a paragraph can measure your pain.
And I won't tell you that healing should be easy.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, protection, community support, and the slow work of recovery.
Some relationships should never return to what they were.
Some wrongs must be brought before lawful authorities.
And some apologies, even sincere ones, cannot undo what happened.
But there is one truth I want you to consider.
The person who wounded you has already taken enough from your life. Don't let hatred take the rest.
You do not have to enjoy their downfall to believe that God is just.
You do not have to destroy them to prove that what happened to you mattered.
You do not have to deny your pain to begin surrendering vengeance.
And you do not have to manufacture warm feelings toward someone who harmed you before you can begin obeying Jesus.
Sometimes loving your enemy begins with a prayer so small it barely feels like a prayer.
"Lord, I don't want to forgive them."
"Lord, I'm angry."
"Lord, I still want them to hurt."
"Lord, I know You command me to love, but I don't know how."
"Lord, help me desire justice without becoming consumed by revenge."
That kind of honesty is not something to hide from God.
He already knows.
Bring it into His presence.
The Psalms contain cries of grief, anger, and appeals for divine judgment. Scripture does not demand that wounded people pretend their pain is unreal.
But it does invite us to place that pain before the Lord instead of enthroning it in our hearts.
And perhaps the first evidence of healing will not be that you suddenly feel affection for your enemy.
Perhaps it will be that you stop checking whether their life has gotten worse.
Perhaps it will be that you refuse to share a humiliating post.
Perhaps it will be that you no longer need everyone else to hate them with you.
Perhaps it will be that you can finally say:
"God, I want the truth to be known. I want those harmed to be protected. I want justice to be done. But if this person truly repents, I will not stand against Your mercy."
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And surrender is often where freedom begins.
There is another truth we must face, especially as believers.
Not everyone who claims to represent Jesus is reflecting His heart.
Jesus said in John 13:35:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples by their ability to win arguments.
Or by the sharpness of their insults.
Or by the speed with which they could expose their enemies.
Truth matters.
Sound doctrine matters.
Righteous judgment matters.
But according to 1 Corinthians 13, even extraordinary spiritual gifts and knowledge become empty when love is absent.
And that should make us tremble before posting something in the name of Christ.
Because it is possible to defend a true doctrine with an unloving spirit.
It is possible to expose a real wrong while indulging in sinful cruelty.
It is possible to win the argument and wound our witness.
It is possible to be applauded by thousands online while grieving the heart of the Savior we profess to follow.
And before we write, "They deserved it," perhaps we should remember what we deserved apart from grace.
Before we type, "God finally punished them," perhaps we should remember how patiently God has dealt with us.
Before we celebrate another person's humiliation, perhaps we should ask whether we would want our own darkest failures broadcast to strangers who were eager to laugh.
This does not mean our sins and their sins are equally harmful in every earthly sense.
They may not be.
Some wrongs inflict devastating damage and demand serious consequences.
But none of us stands before God as someone who has never needed forgiveness.
The ground at the foot of the cross is not a place for boasting.
It is a place for repentance.
And that brings us to the question we cannot avoid.
What would happen if Christians became known not for celebrating the destruction of their enemies, but for telling the truth, defending the vulnerable, pursuing justice, and praying for repentance?
What would happen if we stopped confusing cruelty with courage?
What would happen if we refused to turn every tragedy into an opportunity to humiliate someone?
What would happen if people who had been wounded could find a Church that listened to them, protected them, and walked with them toward healing—without teaching them to hate?
What would happen if those who had committed wrongs encountered believers who demanded accountability but still believed that Christ could transform a repentant sinner?
Maybe the watching world would see something it desperately needs.
Not a Church that excuses evil.
Not a Church that hides scandal.
Not a Church that celebrates suffering.
But a Church that takes sin seriously because it takes the cross seriously.
A Church that understands grace is costly.
A Church that believes redemption is possible because Jesus is alive.
And a Church that remembers that none of us is saved by being more deserving than our enemies.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because consequences are always removed.
Not because every broken relationship is restored in this lifetime.
But because no human story is beyond the reach of Christ's power to redeem those who turn to Him.
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
And the resurrection declares that death, sin, and darkness do not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus.
Perhaps you have spent years praying for God to change the person who hurt you.
Today, perhaps He is inviting you to pray something else as well.
"Lord, change me."
Not because their wrongdoing was acceptable.
Not because your suffering didn't matter.
But because you deserve to live free from the spiritual captivity of bitterness.
And because the Savior who forgave you is worthy of a heart increasingly shaped by His love.
If this article has exposed something you have been carrying, don't hide behind a religious answer.
Be honest.
Perhaps there is someone in your family who needs this message.
Perhaps a friend has been consumed by anger.
Perhaps someone in your church has mistaken public humiliation for righteous judgment.
Perhaps an unbeliever has walked away from Christianity after watching professing Christians celebrate human suffering.

And if you believe messages like this should continue reaching wounded believers, struggling families, seekers, and people who are searching for their way back to Jesus, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Our desire is to help people return to Scripture, understand the Gospel, confront sin honestly, experience the hope of God's grace, and grow in genuine discipleship.

We want those resources and Christ-centered messages to continue reaching people who may never walk into a church building, people who are quietly fighting spiritual battles, and people who need to discover that Jesus has not stopped calling sinners to repentance and new life.
You can help make that mission possible.
These products can become everyday reminders of faith, meaningful gifts, and conversation starters about Jesus.
It is the mission.

It is the possibility that someone scrolling through Facebook at the lowest point of their life may encounter a Scripture-filled message that leads them to open their Bible, seek help, repent, pray, and turn toward Christ.
It is the opportunity to help make biblical encouragement available to people you may never meet.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. Gospel Warrior is simply seeking to serve Him.
Because the world has enough people teaching us how to hate.
It desperately needs to see what happens when human hearts are transformed by the love of Christ.
Before you leave, I want you to picture one final scene.
You are standing at the foot of the cross.
Jesus is suffering.
The crowd is mocking Him.
The innocent Son of God is dying for sinners.
And among the sinners who desperately need His mercy…
Is you.
Is me.
And perhaps even the person you have struggled so hard to forgive.
Suddenly, the question is no longer whether our enemies deserve grace.
The question becomes whether we truly understand the grace that saved us.
Because if Jesus had treated His enemies the way we sometimes want to treat ours, what hope would any of us have?
So the next time someone who hurt you falls, don't be quick to laugh.
Pray for those who have been harmed.
Pray for truth.
Pray for justice.
Pray for genuine repentance.
And ask Jesus to keep your heart from becoming the very thing that wounded you.
You may not be ready to trust that person again.
You may never be reconciled.
You may still need boundaries, accountability, and protection.
But by the grace of God, you do not have to become a prisoner of hatred.

And if you're the one who has done the hurting, don't use this message to demand forgiveness from someone you harmed. Confess your wrongdoing, turn from it, accept appropriate consequences, make restitution where possible, and seek the mercy of Jesus with genuine repentance.
There is grace for the wounded.
There is a call to repentance for the guilty.
And there is a Savior powerful enough to transform both.
So tonight, if an enemy's name rises in your heart, try praying this:

"Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what they did. You know what I have carried. I am not asking You to pretend evil is good. I am asking You to protect me from becoming bitter. Give justice to those who have been wronged. Bring genuine repentance where there has been sin. Heal what has been broken in me. Teach me to love without surrendering truth, to forgive without abandoning wisdom, and to trust Your judgment more than my desire for revenge. And remind me that I stand before You only because of Your mercy. In Your holy name, amen."
And remember this when the old anger returns:
The cross where Jesus died for His enemies is the very place where He calls you to lay down your hatred.
